title: The Rainforest
sources: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute (nationalzoo.si.edu)

cover.artAlt: A lush green rainforest canopy in the morning, with mist rising between tall trees and sunbeams breaking through the leaves
cover.blurb: High above the ground, where sunbeams slip through the misty green leaves, a whole wonderful world is waiting. Turn the page and let us explore the rainforest together.

pages.title: A Beak Bigger Than Its Head
pages.artAlt: A toucan with a huge colorful beak perches on a mossy branch

facts.text: The toucan's beak is so big that it can be four times the size of its head and nearly as long as its whole body. Even so, the bird holds it up with ease. It is one of the most colorful beaks in the entire rainforest.

You might think such a giant beak would be very heavy, but it is surprisingly light. Inside it has a honeycomb pattern full of tiny air pockets, a bit like a sponge. That clever design lets the toucan flit from tree to tree without getting tired.
facts.artAlt: A toucan flies between rainforest trees with its wings spread and its huge orange beak held out ahead of it
facts.caption: A toucan flits from tree to tree without getting tired.

facts.text: A toucan loves to snack on juicy fruit, plucking it with the tip of its long beak. As it flies around, seeds travel inside the bird and are dropped in new places. In this way the toucan helps plant fresh trees all across the forest.
facts.artAlt: A toucan on a branch holds a bright red berry at the very tip of its long beak
facts.caption: Plucking a berry with the very tip of that long beak.

infographic.title: A beak four times the size of its head
infographic.caption: The San Diego Zoo says a toucan's beak can be four times the size of its head. Drawn here in heads, so you can see it without needing a ruler.

pages.title: Where the River Leaps
pages.artAlt: A rainforest waterfall crashes into a clear pool surrounded by green ferns

facts.text: A waterfall often begins where a river flows over two kinds of rock, one soft and one hard. The soft rock slowly wears away, leaving a hard ledge for the water to tumble over. Little by little, over a very long time, the leaping water shapes the waterfall you see today.

At the bottom, the falling water crashes down and swirls around, scooping out a deep dip in the rock. Scientists call this a plunge pool. It is the clear pool where all the tumbling water finally comes to rest.
facts.artAlt: A tall rainforest waterfall drops down a dark rock face into a deep clear pool
facts.caption: All that falling water has scooped out a deep plunge pool.

facts.text: The feathery green ferns around the pool adore this damp, misty spot. Instead of growing from seeds like many plants, ferns grow from tiny specks called spores that need a moist place to sprout. That is why you so often find them close to splashing water.
facts.artAlt: Feathery green ferns grow thickly on wet rocks in the misty spray beside a rainforest pool
facts.caption: Ferns crowd the wet, misty rocks beside the water.

infographic.title: How a waterfall makes itself

stops.label: A river runs over two kinds of rock, one soft and one hard

The falling water scoops out a deep plunge pool below

infographic.caption: This takes far longer than a person's whole life, which is why a waterfall looks like it has always been there.

pages.title: The Little Frog in a Bright Coat
pages.artAlt: A tiny bright red frog sits on a wet green leaf

facts.text: This little frog is truly tiny, often only about the size of a gumdrop, or roughly one inch long. Some kinds are even smaller than that. It can sit happily on a single wet leaf with room to spare.

Its bright red color is not only pretty to look at. To other animals the bold color is like a friendly sign that says please do not eat me. Wearing such cheerful colors is this frog's clever way of staying safe.
facts.artAlt: A brilliant red poison dart frog sits on a glossy wet green leaf, its color vivid against the green
facts.caption: Bright red is a sign that says please do not eat me.

facts.text: For dinner this frog hunts very small creatures such as ants, termites and beetles. It flicks out its tongue to catch them one by one. Even a tiny frog can have a big appetite for bugs.
facts.artAlt: A tiny red frog sits on a mossy log beside a line of small ants
facts.caption: Ants and other tiny bugs are dinner.

infographic.title: How tiny is tiny?
infographic.caption: The frog's length comes from the San Diego Zoo. The everyday sizes are here only so you have something to measure against.

pages.title: The Loudest Voice in the Treetops
pages.artAlt: A howler monkey swings between vines high in the leafy canopy

facts.text: The howler monkey has one of the loudest voices of any animal on land. When it calls out, the deep whooping sound can travel about three miles through the forest. That is a bit like hearing a friend from right across a whole town.
facts.source: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute (nationalzoo.si.edu)

facts.text: High in the branches, the howler monkey has a special helper, and it is its tail. The underside has no hair and can grip like an extra hand, holding tight to branches and vines. This lets the monkey hang on safely as it moves through the treetops.
facts.source: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute (nationalzoo.si.edu)
facts.artAlt: A howler monkey's tail is curled tightly around a thick branch with the monkey hanging below it
facts.caption: The tail grips the branch like an extra hand.

facts.text: Howler monkeys are the largest monkeys in the rainforests of Latin America, and they spend nearly all their time up in the trees. They munch mostly on leaves, plucked fresh from the branches around them. Home for a howler is high above the forest floor.
facts.source: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute (nationalzoo.si.edu)
facts.artAlt: Two howler monkeys sit high in the rainforest canopy eating fresh green leaves
facts.caption: Howler monkeys spend nearly all their time up in the trees.

infographic.title: How far can one howl travel?

A howler monkey calling, about 3 miles
